metadata.title: Judge skeptical of Trump's White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico

sources.news_title: The judge said the outlets may not have received required notice before their access was revoked, and he delayed ruling on a temporary restraining order.
sources.text:
Judge skeptical of White House ban of 3 news outlets but holds off on ruling for now
The White House, south facing, early on the morning of June 11, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — U.S. District Court Judge Timothy J. Kelly indicated during a Wednesday hearing he may order the Trump administration to reinstate White House press passes for reporters from three news organizations who had their credentials revoked this weekend.
Kelly, of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, said at the beginning of a 45-minute hearing that he is largely bound by circuit court rulings that ensure journalists with White House press passes have due process rights before their access to the complex could be rescinded.
“The government says those cases … were wrongly decided,” Kelly said. “Maybe they were, maybe they weren’t. But certainly as a district judge I have to apply them and I think it is fair to say that the processes that the Circuit Court laid out in those two cases … (weren’t) followed here.”
Kelly said at the end of the hearing he will release his ruling as soon as he can, though he did not give any more details about how soon that might be.
President Donald Trump nominated Kelly during his first term and the Senate confirmed him following a broadly bipartisan vote in September 2017.
This case began Monday when CNN, MS Now and Politico sued the Trump administration for barring their reporters from entering the White House grounds.
The news organizations asked the district court to grant them either a temporary restraining order or a preliminary injunction that would require the White House to return the press passes, allowing the journalists to work from the complex once again.
‘Very essence of the First Amendment’
Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., a partner at Gibson Dunn who represented the news organizations, said the president’s decision to revoke the press passes of 78 journalists represented an “unprecedented, unreasonable and severe punishment.”
“What the government is objecting to … is that very essence of the First Amendment,” he said.
Boutrous said claims from the White House the president’s decision was based on national security concerns only came after the lawsuit was filed, not when the decision was announced Friday, or over the weekend when it was implemented.
Trump said Friday in response to questions from reporters in the Oval Office that his ban wasn’t in response to any specific story but “really just cumulative stories over the last two years.”
“They’re smart people, but they purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “And honestly, we’ve done a fantastic job. Look at the numbers, look at the economic numbers. We have more money coming into our country today than ever before.”
Boutrous argued during the hearing that while the president holds the right to criticize reporters and news organizations as much as he wants, the administration cannot “use the power of the government to punish them for their expression.”
In response to questions from the judge about whether there would ever be a circumstance where the White House could revoke a press pass, Boutrous said if someone was a spy, represented a physical threat, or a national security threat, “there would of course be authority by the White House to deal with that.”
But he also referenced the Pentagon Papers, and said he didn’t believe that type of reporting on national security issues would justify revoking a reporter’s White House press pass.
The White House’s decision to revoke press passes for reporters from those three news organizations has led the major television networks that rotate daily coverage of the president to stop doing so. The decision has limited what videos of the president are released through that television pool system.
DOJ argues access ‘a privilege, not a right’
Michael Velchik, senior counsel in the civil division of the Justice Department, said the Trump administration would oppose a ruling requiring the White House to return the press passes and allow reporters from those news organizations to resume coverage there.
“Access to the White House is a privilege not a right,” he said.
Velchik seemed to suggest that if the judge were to require the White House to reinstate the press passes, it shouldn’t happen during the next few days, when Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to be in Washington, D.C., to meet with the president.
The White House, he said, had also sent letters to CNN, MS Now and Politico on Tuesday, informing them why their press passes were revoked and giving them the chance to reply by Friday evening.
Democrat sees ban as part of pattern
U.S. House Administration Committee ranking member Joe Morelle, D-N.Y., said during a separate virtual press briefing on Wednesday that he believes the ban of the news outlets was part of a pattern of Trump misusing government power to attack perceived opponents.
“The Trump administration has flagrantly abused the immense power of the federal government against organizations and institutions whose work, whose clients or viewpoints it disagrees with,” he said. “We don’t need to look any further than this outrageous attempt by the president to silence CNN, MS Now, Politico and others.”
Jacob Fischler contributed to this report.

A federal judge has heard complaints from CNN, MSNOW and Politico about President Donald Trump’s decision to ban them from the White House over biased reporting, and has promised to make a decision.
But not immediately, as the lawsuit plaintiffs had insisted.
Meanwhile, commentator and longtime media expert Brit Hume noted that the biased reports were just that, in fact, they were “comically unbalanced.”
Trump earlier banished AP reporters form some parts of the White House because the organization insisted on calling what he had designated as the Gulf of America the Gulf of Mexico.
Trump’s decision was affirmed by a federal judge.
Now the various corporations are challenging Trump’s decision to banish “fake news” reporters.
He, in fact, has explained that such negative coverage as the organizations have delivered actually is dangerous for the country.
Judge Timothy Kelly heard the lawsuit by the media groups, but didn’t rule immediately.

Previous court precedent has said that “reporters” must have an opportunity to be heard before their passes are revoked.
Lawyer Theodore Boutrous Jr. told the court the banishment is “unreasonable punishment.”
The White House has pointed out it is not obstructing any of the reporting duties by the individuals involved, it just isn’t allowing them at the White House, a location that is controlled by the president.
The administration has told the court the reporting by the outlets violated “standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues and publishing sensitive or classified information.”
It confirmed that letters were dispatched to the organizations identifying “a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents, including that that have threatened national security and spread falsehoods.”
Trump has given the organizations until Friday to respond to his accusations of “reported national security breaches.”
Trump has said, “I think we have a right to clean out fake news.”
Other news organizations, claiming solidarity, have since declined to do some of the First Amendment reporting they otherwise might have, they said.
Brit Hume’s opinion was clear:

The lawyers for CNN and MS NOW say that President Donald Trump is basically their "lead witness" in their case to sink his media ban.
On Wednesday, U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, heard the case against Trump's media ban as he considered a temporary restraining order to block it. CNN, MS NOW and Politico were all kicked out of the White House by the media ban, but lawyers said their strategy hinged on using Trump's words against him.
Politico legal reporter Kyle Cheney wrote in a post on X, "Lawyer for Politico, CNN, MS NOW Ted Boutrous says President Trump is basically 'our lead witness' because he keeps making plain why the ban happened: he doesn't like the outlets' coverage."
Cheney reported in a Politico article that Kelly indicated early in the hearing that "Trump's effort to strip credentials from Politico, CNN and MS NOW appeared to violate binding legal precedents requiring that journalists have advance notice of the rules they must observe."
However, during the hearing, Kelly said that the legal precedent "wasn't followed here," according to Politico. Cheney expanded on Kelly's words in a post on X, where Cheney wrote that Kelly "imediately makes clear he's bound by D.C. Circuit precedent that upholds due process protections for WH reporters who hold hard passes."
Kelly said, "I think it is fair to say that the process" wasn't followed, per Cheney. In his Politico article, Cheney wrote that Kelly "appeared skeptical" about ruling in favor of Trump.
NYU Law professor and CNN legal analyst Ryan Goodman had a stronger read of the hearing, writing in a post on X that the "White House will lose on clear violation of due process when fundamental First Amendment interest at stake." Goodman posted his analysis on X just minutes after the hearing ended.
"DOJ had no answer to Judge Kelly's points about precedent requiring government to provide standards prior to alleged misconduct," Goodman pointed out. "None."

Judge: Trump’s White House media ban may violate legal precedents
WASHINGTON >> A U.S. judge told a hearing on Wednesday that President Donald Trump’s decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House did not appear to comply with prior rulings by a federal appellate court, but did not issue an immediate ruling on whether the news outlets should have their access restored.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly held the hearing in Washington to consider a request by the news outlets for a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while a legal challenge they filed on Monday plays out.
The outlets said the ban violated the U.S. Constitution’s First Amendment protections for freedom of speech and a free press as well as their rights to due process.
The judge said that two precedents from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit make clear that journalists are entitled to due process before their White House press passes can be revoked. The judge added that it did not appear that the White House had given the three news outlets a meaningful opportunity to contest the revocation of their access.
“The government said those cases … were wrongly decided,” Kelly said. “Maybe they were wrongly decided, maybe they weren’t. But as a district court judge I have to apply them. I think it is fair to say the process the circuit laid out in those two cases wasn’t followed here.”
Kelly said he would issue a ruling at a later time on the request for a temporary restraining order.

A lawyer for the news outlets told Kelly that they were banned without legally required advance notice or opportunity to contest the decisions.
“By ejecting and banning the plaintiffs from the White House without a semblance of due process here, defendants have imposed what really amounts to an unprecedented, unreasonable and severe punishment,” attorney Theodore Boutrous said.
Michael Velchik, a Justice Department lawyer, told the judge the Trump administration provided a sufficient explanation for the revocation of the press passes in letters sent to the news outlets on Tuesday. But the judge signaled skepticism of that argument, noting that the letters were sent after the revocation occurred and the lawsuit was filed.
“I don’t know how a letter that they got after the pass was revoked could provide them with the notice of the kind of standards that they would have to conform their conduct to, since it’s a piece of paper they got saying, ‘You’ve already violated this.’”
In a legal filing on the eve of the hearing, the Justice Department argued that access to the White House is a privilege, not an entitlement, and that the president had the authority to suspend access by news organizations. The department also echoed Trump’s contention that the bans are justified by national security concerns regarding news coverage by the outlets.
The news outlets have accused Trump of unlawful discrimination against them based on their viewpoints.
“The viewpoint discrimination is probably the clearest case in history. I mean, the president said, ‘I don’t like what you’re publishing. I’m taking away your press pass based on that,’” Boutrous told the hearing.
“They are using national security as this talisman — these magic words,” Boutrous said. “It is just a pretextual, post hoc effort to justify just a blatant violation of due process.”
Trump announced the ban on Friday on his social media platform, saying those news organizations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.”
The government on Tuesday said it sent letters to the outlets after the ban that accused them of endangering national security with their reporting, citing stories about U.S. missile stockpiles, construction of Trump’s White House ballroom and turnout at the Republican Party’s recent midterm convention.
“The president has set out notice of his determination that he personally made to identify this particularity and not exhaustive list of reporting incidents. He has provided a process for plaintiffs to contest these particular incidents,” Velchik told the judge.
But Boutrous said, “It’s not due process when there is a prejudgment of the issues.”
In a 2018 case that raised similar legal issues, Kelly ordered the White House to restore CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s press pass, which had been revoked after a contentious news conference with Trump. Kelly ruled in that case that the White House had not used fair and clear procedures to revoke Acosta’s credential, calling the process “shrouded in mystery.”
In a social media post on Monday, Trump indicated regret over appointing Kelly to the bench in 2017, during his first term as president, and said he was bracing for a loss.
A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organizations filed a legal brief on Wednesday supporting the three news outlets targeted by Trump. They asserted that “stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of Supreme Court jurisprudence and is impermissible in any type of forum, including the White House.”
The brief was signed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Reuters, the Washington Post and Fox News, among others.
